title: Vectors
bridge: C++'s growable list is `std::vector<T>` from `<vector>`: `std::vector<int> v = {4, 5, 6}; v.push_back(7); v.size(); v[0];`. Loop with `for (int x : v)`. Pass vectors to functions as `const std::vector<int>& v` so they aren't copied.
lesson:
```
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> scores = {72, 85, 90};
scores.push_back(64);        // add to the end -> 4 items
scores.size();               // 4
scores[0];                   // 72
scores.back();               // 64
scores.pop_back();           // remove the last
scores.empty();              // false

int total = 0;
for (int s : scores) total += s;
```

**Passing to functions.** Written as `std::vector<int> v`, the whole vector is *copied* every call, which is slow for big ones. Write `const std::vector<int>& v` instead: the `&` means "use the original", and `const` promises not to change it. You'll see this pattern everywhere in C++ and in Unreal (`const TArray<AActor*>& Targets`).

`v[i]` doesn't check `i` is valid: reading `v[10]` of a 3-item vector is **undefined behaviour** (garbage, or a crash). `v.at(10)` checks and throws an error instead.

Unreal's version is `TArray` (`Add`, `Num`, `[i]`); Unity's C# version is `List<T>`. Same idea everywhere.

exercises.title: Average of a vector
exercises.prompt: Write double average(const std::vector<int>& v): the average, or 0 for an empty vector.

tests.hint_if_fail: Divide as a double, not as ints.
An empty vector has size 0: don't divide by it.

hints: Add them up in a loop, then divide by v.size().

exercises.title: Count above a limit
exercises.prompt: Write int countAbove(const std::vector<int>& v, int limit): how many items are greater than limit.
hints: for (int x : v) if (x > limit) n++;
